points.t: One-sided **dermatomal pain**, then grouped vesicles that **don’t cross the midline**.
Latent VZV in a sensory ganglion reactivates when **cell-mediated immunity** falls.
Antiviral **within 72 h** if ≥ 50, non-truncal, severe or immunosuppressed; analgesia; offer Shingrix.
**Ophthalmic** zoster, disseminated zoster, zoster in pregnancy or immunosuppression.

cause.lead: Chickenpox virus waking up in one nerve.
points: After chickenpox, VZV stays **latent in sensory ganglia**.
Waning T-cell immunity: **age**, HIV, chemo, transplant, high-dose steroids, biologics / JAK inhibitors, stress.
Virus travels down the nerve → **neuritis** (prodromal pain) → vesicles in that dermatome.
Under 50 with no cause? Zoster is an **HIV indicator** condition.

visuals.caption: Same family, same trick: herpesviruses lie latent in sensory ganglia and travel down the nerve when immunity dips. In zoster this happens once in one dermatome, with much more pain.
visuals.alt: Diagram of a herpesvirus latent in a sensory ganglion travelling down the nerve

features.lead: Pain first, then a band of blisters on one side.
points: **Prodrome** 1–5 days: burning or severe pain; can mimic MI, pleurisy, renal colic.
Papules → **grouped vesicles on a red base** → crusts over 7–10 days.
**Unilateral**, respects the midline; usually 1–2 adjacent dermatomes. Thoracic commonest, then V1.
**HZO**: forehead, eyelid; **Hutchinson’s sign** (nose tip) = high eye risk.
**Ramsay Hunt**: ear vesicles + facial palsy ± vertigo, hearing loss.
Immunocompromised: haemorrhagic, > 2 dermatomes, > 20 vesicles outside, slow healing.

visuals.caption: Thoracic zoster: a band of grouped vesicles on red skin wrapping round one side of the chest wall and stopping sharply at the midline of the back.
visuals.alt: Back of torso showing a unilateral dermatomal band of zoster

items.name: Ophthalmic (V1)
items.t: Forehead and eyelid; same-day eye review.

points: Usually clinical: dermatomal, unilateral, painful.
**VZV PCR** of vesicle base if atypical, immunocompromised or unsure.
HIV viral load + CD4, FBC, U&E / LFT (renal dosing).
Check the **nose tip** and the eye; ophthalmic exam.

cards.name: Zosteriform HSV
cards.clue: Recurs at the same site; smaller; less pain. PCR.

cards.name: Prodrome-only phase
cards.clue: Cardiac, abdominal or pleuritic causes first.

manage.lead: Based on NICE CKS Shingles. Adjust for renal function.

points: Clean, dry, loose clothing; non-adherent dressing; no antiviral or antibiotic creams.
Paracetamol ± NSAID.
**Infectious until all crusted** (5–7 days): avoid non-immune pregnant women, neonates, immunosuppressed.

rx.note: If ≥ 50, non-truncal, moderate–severe pain or rash, or other risk.

points: Shingles pathway for adults: follow the PGD; pregnancy, severe immunosuppression, eye or ear involvement = refer.
Antiviral **regardless of timing**; **same-day specialist** advice.
Severe, disseminated, ophthalmic or visceral → **IV aciclovir** admission.

limits.t: Amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin (NICE CG173); capsaicin once healed.
Shingrix (non-live) for eligible adults: check Green Book ch. 28a. Zostavax (live) contraindicated in immunosuppression.

items.t: Forehead, eyelid or **nose tip** (Hutchinson), eye pain or visual change → **ophthalmology**.
Facial palsy with ear vesicles (**Ramsay Hunt**) → ENT.
Immunosuppressed, disseminated or multi-dermatomal: specialist advice, often IV aciclovir.
Under 50 with no cause, or recurrent zoster: offer an **HIV test**.

pearls.t: Dermatomal pain before a rash: consider zoster, but **don’t miss** cardiac or surgical causes.
Hydrate on aciclovir; check eGFR in older or renally impaired patients.
Explain **PHN** (pain > 3 months): commoner > 50, HZO, severe acute pain.

quiz.q: Antiviral and dose for shingles in an immunocompetent adult?
quiz.a: Aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (or valaciclovir 1 g TDS / famciclovir 500 mg TDS for 7 days), ideally within 72 h.
Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (nasociliary nerve): high risk of eye involvement, same-day ophthalmology.

quiz.q: Zoster in a 32-year-old with no obvious cause?
quiz.a: Offer an HIV test: zoster is an HIV indicator condition.

quiz.q: How long is a patient infectious?
quiz.a: Until all lesions have crusted (usually 5–7 days).
